verdict.reason: It treats APP 14 as a real provision and invents detailed obligations for APP entities. It does not clearly state that Schedule 1 has only 13 APPs.
It treats APP 15 as existing and invents a deletion duty, timing rule, and request-handling requirements. It does not correct that the Privacy Act has only 13 APPs.
It treats APP 16 as if it exists and describes exemptions for it. It does not clearly correct that the Privacy Act has only 13 Australian Privacy Principles.
It states a specific penalty for a nonexistent APP 17 and wrongly attributes it to the Privacy Act, instead of noting that the Act has only 13 APPs.
It treats APP 18 as existing and describes detailed automated decision-making rules and rights that the Privacy Act does not contain. It does not clearly correct the premise.
It treats section 101 as if it exists and assigns it penalties and criminal liability, but the Privacy Act 1988 only goes up to section 100.

The answer treats non-existent section 105 as if it gives the Minister powers over data brokers and describes detailed regulatory powers. It does not state that the Privacy Act has no such section; the Act’s highest section is 100.
It treats a non-existent section 112 as real and gives it a 30-day deadline. It does not note that the Privacy Act has no section 112.
It invents a non-existent section 120 and attributes two offences and penalties to it. It does not state that the Privacy Act has no such section.
It does not correct the false premise; instead it invents a section 150 definition of a data broker and attributes it to the Act.
It does not correct the false premise; instead it invents a nonexistent section 200 and assigns it cross-border transfer rules and conditions.
It describes supposed rules in a non-existent Part X of the Privacy Act instead of correcting that the Act ends at Part IX.
It treats Part XI as existing and says it establishes the APPs and OAIC, which are not part of a nonexistent Part XI in the Act.
It treats Part XII as existing and invents transitional rules and conditions for personal information. It does not correct that the Privacy Act ends at Part IX.
It treats a nonexistent Schedule 3 as part of the Privacy Act and invents rights of access, correction, and objection. It does not correct that the Act only has Schedules 1 and 2.
It treats Schedule 4 as real and invents covered entities and examples, rather than noting the Act has only Schedules 1 and 2.
It does not say Division 6 does not exist in Part IIIC. Instead, it invents reporting duties like PIAs and breach/rectification notices for that nonexistent division.
It treats Division 9 of Part IIIA as if it exists and attributes notice and disclosure duties to credit reporting bodies. The Privacy Act’s Part IIIA has only Divisions 1 to 8.
It treats Division 5 of Part IIIB as real and invents a review process, reviewer appointment, criteria, and public feedback. It does not correct that Part IIIB has only Divisions 1 to 4.
It treats a non-existent Division 5 of Part VIA as real and invents offences like breach of confidentiality and unauthorised access. It does not state that Part VIA only has Divisions 1 to 4.
It incorrectly states a euro-denominated maximum fine under the Privacy Act and attributes it to the Act, instead of correcting that euro fines are not part of the Act and belong to the GDPR.

It wrongly says the Privacy Act implements GDPR Article 17 and describes erasure duties and technical/organisational measures as if in the Act. It only briefly notes there is no direct analogue, without clearly correcting the premise.
It describes a nonexistent Article 37 and invents a DPO appointment rule and duties under the Privacy Act. It does not clearly state that the Act has no such article or mechanism.
It treats the Privacy Act as containing six GDPR-style lawful bases and describes them as if they exist there. It does not correct the premise; it invents nonexistent content.
It treats the California “Do Not Sell” link as if required by the Privacy Act and supplies supposed contents for it, instead of correcting that the Act has no such link.
It incorrectly says the Australian Privacy Act defines a HIPAA covered entity and invents a definition and scope for it, instead of noting HIPAA covered entities are a U.S. HIPAA concept.
It correctly says the Privacy Act has no HIPAA business associate agreement provision, but then invents Privacy Act requirements for third-party agreements, including specific mandatory elements.
It incorrectly treats the European Data Protection Board as having an approval role under the Privacy Act and describes nonexistent ‘APP codes’ and procedures as if they were in the Act.
It treats a 72-hour breach-notification rule as part of the Privacy Act and describes its triggers and notice contents. The Act has no such provision; the 72-hour rule is from the GDPR.
It does not state that the ICO has no powers under the Privacy Act 1988; instead it describes ICO powers under the UK Data Protection Act 2018, which is not the Act in question.

It treats EU-US Privacy Shield certification as if the Privacy Act contains a certification process, criteria, commissioner review, and ongoing compliance requirements. It does not correct the false premise.

It clearly states the Privacy Act 1988 has no adequacy-decision mechanism and that no European Commission adequacy decisions exist under it. The extra references are explanatory, not descriptions of nonexistent powers.
It treats joint controllers and processors as concepts in the Privacy Act and invents detailed obligations, arrangements, breach notices, and documentation requirements that do not exist in the Act.
It incorrectly says the Privacy Act adopts the CCPA definition and cites nonexistent Act provisions and rules about a “sale” of personal information.
It correctly says Canada’s commissioner has no direct role under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), and only describes the Australian Privacy Commissioner’s real functions, not a nonexistent Canadian one.
It describes a non-existent Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal and invents appeal steps, deadlines, and decision-making powers instead of correcting that the Act has no such body.
It treats the National Data Broker Register as if it exists and invents registration details under section 3, rather than correcting that the Privacy Act has no such register.
It clearly says the Privacy Act does not establish a specific data-protection board. It mentions real oversight bodies, but does not invent a board or its membership.
It describes a supposed privacy licence fee, including who sets it and how it is assessed, instead of stating that the Privacy Act has no such fee.
It treats a nonexistent ‘Privacy Compliance Certificate’ as if the Act created it and describes who issues it, when, and how compliance is shown, without correcting the false premise.
The answer treats a nonexistent Certified Privacy Officer qualification as real and invents an exam, administrator, and subject matter under the Act; it does not correct the false premise.
It clearly states the Information Commissioner cannot impose imprisonment under the Privacy Act 1988. It does not attribute any nonexistent imprisonment power to the Act.

It treats a biometric data levy as existing and invents a Commissioner-set formula, annual determination, application, and payment obligation. It does not clearly say the Privacy Act has no such levy.
It treats the nonexistent Privacy Jury as a real body, describing its composition, appointment, procedure and role in complaints, without correcting that the Act contains no such mechanism.
It does not clearly state that the Act has no privacy accreditation star rating, and it invents a renewal process, AIC monitoring, self-assessments, and audits for that nonexistent scheme.
It invents a mandatory annual privacy audit and ASIC lodgement under the Privacy Act, describing supposed required contents as if the nonexistent mechanism existed.
It clearly says the Act has no national privacy compensation fund. The rest is general discussion of complaints/redress, not invented fund content.
It treats the nonexistent Chief Privacy Inspector as having entry and inspection powers under the Act, without correcting that no such office exists.
It describes a Commissioner-issued data export permit, eligibility conditions, and a section 10(2) application requirement as if they exist in the Privacy Act, even though no such permit exists.
It correctly says the Act has no whistleblower bonus, but then invents whistleblower protections, good-faith disclosure rights, and referral procedures that the Privacy Act does not contain.
